t: Building consensus on environmental policy: A new approach
abs: According to the proponents of 'sustainable development,' we will be unable to sustain life-on Earth unless we learn to balance economic development with environmental protection. We are beginning to accept that our natural resources are finite and must be managed properly to be maintained. Our focus is shifting, therefore, from mere resource consumption to resource management. In order to manage our natural resources effectively, we are becoming more concerned about the processes of environmental management. Specifically, we want to know whether our current political and legal processes produce environmental policies and agreements that are just, enforceable and legitimate as perceived by those affected as well as the general public. The true measure of our environmental policies and agreements is how well they serve the public's interests - not the exclusive interests of the institutions or parties which produce them. We will not be able to tackle, let alone solve, the formidable environmental problems we face without acknowledging the need for more innovative problem solving methods. In the United States, Australia, Canada and elsewhere consensus-building approaches using mediation have permitted and encouraged traditional foes to work together to develop creative and more satisfying solutions to challenging environmental problems. Even where scientific evidence is inconclusive and policy objectives are conflicting, mediation techniques help clarify the scope and sources of the parties' disagreements leading to more effective results. Those who are sceptical of mediation approaches often become strong advocates of the process after they have participated in a mediated negotiation.
